title: Embedded inference, patch workflow & HW constraints - LumenCare intake
summary: Discovery focused on deploying Redwood in an air-gapped hospital environment. Main concerns: offline patching/update workflow, hardware compatibility (older NVIDIA clusters + upcoming H100s), driver/OS constraints, KMS/HSM integration for keys, auditability (SOC2-like expectations), and pilot success metrics. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share offline update runbook, quantization/benchmark guidance for A100 vs H100, and draft pilot statement of work.
topics: hardware sizing and compatibility (A100, H100, older blades)
keys and secrets (KMS, HSM, key rotation)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE, and with me is Ravi, our solutions engineer. Quick round-robin?
[00:08] Daniel Ortiz: Daniel here, CTO at LumenCare. Priya and Sofia are with me, and Evan.
[00:12] Priya Rao: Hi all.
[00:14] Sofia Martinez: Good afternoon.
[00:15] Ravi Patel: Awesome. Thanks. High level, Maya, do you want to frame what we'll cover?
[00:20] Maya Chen: Sure. Today we want to understand your constraints for an on-prem, air-gapped inference deployment — particularly how you want updates to be applied, any hardware constraints, and compliance requirements. We'll also outline a pilot approach.
[00:34] Daniel Ortiz: Great. To be explicit, this is for models that will do clinical note summarization and triage routing inside hospital networks, so PHI is in scope. We cannot send PHI off-network.
[00:46] Maya Chen: Understood. A few clarifying q's up front: are you targeting fully disconnected operations or periodic controlled updates via removable media?
[00:53] Priya Rao: Periodic controlled updates. We have strict change control. Typically we bring media into a secure room, scan, and apply patches via internal jump host. No persistent outbound internet allowed.
[01:06] Ravi Patel: Got it. So our private deployment pattern for air-gapped sites maps to that—Redwood private with an offline update bundle and signed artifacts. You mentioned jump hosts; can you say more about how you handle attestation and checksums today?
[01:20] Priya Rao: We use SHA256 checks and a separate RMA server that verifies signatures. Our security team insists on HSM-backed signing for production binaries.
[01:29] Sofia Martinez: Also audit logs need to be retained for 7 years and be exportable for e-discovery.
[01:36] Maya Chen: Thanks — that helps. We support signing bundles and we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management. We will need to confirm exact HSM vendor compatibility; those integrations are typically through PKCS#11 or a supported REST KMS if networked.
[01:49] Daniel Ortiz: Question — do you require any outbound callback to Redwood control plane during runtime? Or can the runtime be fully self-contained?
[01:58] Ravi Patel: In air-gapped mode, runtime is fully self-contained for inference. The control plane for management is optional; we provide a control plane that can be installed as a private control plane inside your VPC if you want. For fully disconnected sites, the control plane can be offline and updates applied via signed bundle.
[02:15] Evan Chu: When you say signed bundle, is that a tarball with containers, or some other artifact? How do you handle kernel/driver dependencies?
[02:25] Ravi Patel: Typically an update bundle contains the runtime binaries, model artifacts, and a manifest. For GPUs we provide recipes and checks for driver versions; we don't package vendor drivers themselves due to licensing, but we have exact driver/kernel versions we test against and we can provide a pre-check script that runs on the host to validate compatibility.
[02:44] Priya Rao: We're currently running a mix. A lot of our older racks are A100-based on RHEL 7 with older drivers. We're planning a refresh to H100 nodes over the next 6 months but procurement windows are long.
[02:56] Maya Chen: Important to know. There are runtime differences — H100 and A100 have different kernel optimizations and MHA support; also quantized kernels can behave differently. We can provide a quantization profile and guidance for each card family.
[03:10] Daniel Ortiz: Another constraint: change windows are midnight-2am on weekends only, and we need a rollback path.
[03:17] Ravi Patel: We build bundles with a built-in rollback manifest and a health-check probe that marks a rollout healthy or triggers a rollback. For offline scenarios the operator triggers the bundle install; our tooling will run the pre-checks and after-install probes locally.
[03:30] Sofia Martinez: For compliance, we'll need proof of what's been installed, a signed audit trail, and a way to show model versioning tied to training data snapshots.
[03:40] Maya Chen: We can produce signed deployment manifests showing model version, hash, safety/eval reports, and a human-readable change log. Those artifacts can be signed with your HSM-backed key.
[03:51] Evan Chu: Performance question — if we have older A100s, what's a realistic throughput for our summarization workload? Our docs: average sequence length ~800 tokens, concurrency 6-8 users per device.
[04:05] Ravi Patel: Rough rough ballpark: with optimized kernels and batching, an A100 can handle X tokens/s — (note: rough numbers) for 800 tokens median, expect tail latencies 400–700ms per request depending on batching and KV cache. We should run a short benchmark with your typical prompts. H100 will be faster and more cost-effective per token, but there are tuning differences.
[04:29] Priya Rao: We can't install perf tooling that phones home. Any benchmark needs to be self-contained and produce a report we can review offline.
[04:37] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We can deliver a containerized benchmarking harness and a results tarball that you can run whatever environment you like.
[04:44] Daniel Ortiz: Let me push on a few specifics: keys. We use an on-prem Thales HSM. We rotate keys every quarter, and a custodian signs updates. Does Redwood support using customer-provided HSM for signing and decrypting model artifacts?
[04:58] Ravi Patel: Yes, we can integrate with customer HSM for signing and for key-wrapping the model weights. We'll work with PKCS#11 or a signed bundle approach. Need to confirm Thales model and firmware but we have prior customers on Thales.
[05:12] Sofia Martinez: And what about telemetry? What data leaves the site? We require explicit allowlist and data minimization — no payloads including PHI can be exfiltrated.
[05:23] Maya Chen: For fully air-gapped installs, nothing leaves the site. For private control plane installs in VPC with egress, we can configure telemetry to send only metrics (aggregated counts, health pings) and never payloads; we also support an opt-out. Any telemetry for hosted Redwood is obviously not permitted here.
[05:38] Evan Chu: Okay. I want to understand the update cadence: security patches vs model updates. Our process requires security patches applied within 30 days of release and model updates on a quarterly cadence after validation. Do you support splitting those flows?
[05:52] Ravi Patel: Yes. We recommend separating runtime security patches (OS/drivers) from model rollout bundles. Runtime patches can be validated by your OS team; our pre-flight checks will ensure the runtime is compatible. Model updates are separate signed artifacts that can be applied independently.
[06:06] Daniel Ortiz: Any guidance on immutable infrastructure versus live updates? Our infra team prefers immutable if possible to reduce config drift.
[06:14] Maya Chen: We support both. For immutable, you can bake images with the runtime and model, and then swap nodes. For live updates, the bundle installer runs the deployment and handles state migration. Both approaches have tradeoffs with downtime and rollback complexity.
[06:27] Priya Rao: Budgets question — do you have ballpark pricing for dedicated capacity vs private on-prem licensing?
[06:33] Maya Chen: For private on-prem, pricing is typically a platform license plus support; dedicated is a reserved capacity contract. We'll send a tailored SOW and pricing sheet after we scope hardware and SLOs.
[06:44] Daniel Ortiz: For pilot, we want to test in our staging cluster first, with non-PHI data, then a small production pilot in a single hospital. Success criteria: latency under 1s p50 for summarization, zero data exfiltration, and smooth offline update workflow.
[06:59] Ravi Patel: That's reasonable. We'll propose a pilot that includes an offline update dry-run, a benchmarking harness, and a security runbook for your team to validate.
[07:09] Maya Chen: Quick note on models/quantization: if you want the smallest footprint for older hardware, we recommend int8 or 4-bit qconfigs and our quantization guidance; accuracy regressions will be measured in the eval reports we include.
[07:22] Evan Chu: How do we validate quality regressions? We have a small labeled prompt set.
[07:27] Ravi Patel: Bring us the prompt set; we can run pairwise evals and produce a delta report. All evals can be run offline in your environment or we can run them on Redwood test infra and share results — given PHI concerns, offline is preferred.
[07:40] Sofia Martinez: Any certifications you can point to? SOC 2? ISO?
[07:44] Maya Chen: Redwood has SOC 2 — we'll share the report. For air-gapped private installs, certification evidence is typically the customer's responsibility, but we support audit needs with logs and artefacts.
[07:55] Daniel Ortiz: Last technical nit — our kernel is custom-patched for a specific NV driver backport. Will Redwood support those kernels?
[08:03] Ravi Patel: We can support non-standard kernels via vendor matrix testing, but edge cases require a short compatibility engagement. We can run our pre-checks to see if there are conflicts; if necessary we'll recommend a minimal kernel change or driver patch.
[08:17] Maya Chen: Ok let's capture action items.
[08:19] Maya Chen: Next steps: Redwood will share an offline update runbook, benchmarking harness, quantization guidance per GPU family, and a draft pilot SOW. LumenCare will share a small evaluation prompt set and details of Thales HSM model and firmware.
[08:33] Priya Rao: We'll also share the pre-approved vendor list and change window calendar.
[08:37] Daniel Ortiz: Timeline — want to kick pilot in staging in 6 weeks? Procurement for new hardware is longer but staging is ready.
[08:44] Maya Chen: 6 weeks is plausible for a staging bench test. We'll aim for that and follow up with a SOW.
[08:50] Sofia Martinez: Anything else?
[08:51] Evan Chu: One more: can you provide an example signed audit artifact so our auditors can preview format?
[08:57] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll drop an example signed manifest (sanitized) in the share.
[09:02] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials.
[09:05] Daniel Ortiz: Thanks folks.
[09:06] End of recording.
